concepts.name: Compiler versus interpreter distinction
concepts.summary: Explain how a compiler translates a whole program to another form before running while an interpreter executes the program directly, and that many implementations mix both.

concepts.name: Phases of translation pipeline
concepts.summary: Describe the sequence from source text through lexing, parsing, analysis and code generation to output, and what each phase consumes and produces.

concepts.name: Tokens and lexemes
concepts.summary: Recall that a lexer groups characters into tokens such as identifiers, keywords, literals and operators, discarding whitespace and comments.

concepts.name: Grammar as language specification
concepts.summary: Understand that a grammar with terminals, nonterminals and productions defines which token sequences are valid programs.

concepts.name: Syntax tree structure
concepts.summary: Understand that program structure is represented as a tree where operators and constructs are nodes and operands are children.

concepts.name: Syntax versus semantics errors
concepts.summary: Distinguish errors in program form (syntax) from errors in meaning (such as undeclared variables or type mismatches) and runtime errors.

concepts.name: Machine code, bytecode, and targets
concepts.summary: Name the kinds of output a compiler can produce, including native machine code, bytecode and another high-level language.

misconceptions.text: A language is either compiled or interpreted, as an inherent property of the language itself.
A compiler only checks syntax and does not look at the meaning of the program.
The lexer understands program structure such as nested expressions.

concepts.name: Regular expressions for tokens
concepts.summary: Describe token classes with regular expressions and relate them to finite automata that recognise them.

concepts.name: Writing a hand-coded lexer
concepts.summary: Implement a scanner that reads characters and emits tokens with type, text and position, using longest-match for operators and keywords.

concepts.name: Abstract syntax tree design
concepts.summary: Define node types for expressions and statements that keep meaning and drop punctuation and grouping tokens.

concepts.name: Recursive descent parsing
concepts.summary: Write a parser with one function per grammar rule that consumes tokens and builds an abstract syntax tree.

concepts.name: Operator precedence and associativity
concepts.summary: Encode precedence and associativity in the grammar or with precedence climbing so expressions parse into the correct tree.

concepts.name: Tree-walking evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate an AST by recursively visiting nodes to compute values and carry out statements.

concepts.name: Environments and variable scope
concepts.summary: Store variable bindings in nested environments so lookups and assignments respect block scope.

concepts.name: Syntax error reporting
concepts.summary: Report errors with line and column and recover enough to continue and report further errors.

misconceptions.text: Precedence is handled by the evaluator, so the parser can build any tree shape for an expression.
A recursive descent parser can handle any grammar, including left-recursive rules, without changes.
The AST should keep every token from the source, including parentheses and semicolons.

concepts.name: Grammar ambiguity and LL/LR
concepts.summary: Analyse a grammar for ambiguity, left recursion and lookahead conflicts, and decide whether LL(k) or LR parsing suits it.

concepts.name: Bottom-up shift-reduce parsing
concepts.summary: Trace a shift-reduce parse using a stack and tables, and interpret shift/reduce conflicts reported by a parser generator.

concepts.name: Symbol tables and name resolution
concepts.summary: Build symbol tables during a pass over the AST to resolve each name to its declaration and detect undeclared or duplicate names.

concepts.name: Static type checking
concepts.summary: Apply typing rules to expressions and statements to detect mismatches and annotate the tree with types.

concepts.name: Intermediate representations
concepts.summary: Lower an AST into a linear IR such as three-address code with temporaries and labelled jumps.

concepts.name: Control flow graphs
concepts.summary: Partition IR into basic blocks and connect them into a graph that shows all possible execution paths.

concepts.name: Stack-based bytecode virtual machine
concepts.summary: Compile an AST to stack bytecode and run it in a dispatch loop, and compare this with tree walking.

concepts.name: Runtime call stack and frames
concepts.summary: Analyse how activation records hold arguments, locals and return addresses to implement function calls and recursion.

misconceptions.text: Any grammar that accepts the right programs is fine for a parser, since ambiguity only affects performance.
Static type checking can be skipped for dynamic languages because they have no notion of types.
A bytecode VM is always faster than a tree-walking interpreter regardless of design.

concepts.name: Data-flow analysis
concepts.summary: Formulate forward and backward data-flow problems over the CFG and solve them iteratively to a fixed point.

concepts.name: Static single assignment form
concepts.summary: Analyse how SSA gives each variable one definition, using phi nodes at merges, to simplify optimisations.

concepts.name: Local and global optimisations
concepts.summary: Judge when optimisations such as constant propagation, dead code elimination and inlining are safe and worthwhile.

concepts.name: Register allocation
concepts.summary: Analyse how live ranges, interference and spilling determine register assignment, and compare graph colouring with linear scan.

concepts.name: Instruction selection and calling conventions
concepts.summary: Map IR operations to target instructions and conform to the ABI for argument passing, stack layout and saved registers.

concepts.name: Type inference and polymorphism
concepts.summary: Evaluate unification-based inference and generic implementation strategies such as monomorphisation versus boxing.

concepts.name: Closures and first-class functions
concepts.summary: Analyse how captured variables are stored so functions outlive their defining scope, including heap-allocated environments.

concepts.name: Garbage collection strategies
concepts.summary: Compare mark-sweep, copying, generational and reference-counting collectors by cost, pauses and handling of cycles.

misconceptions.text: An optimisation that speeds up one benchmark is always valid and beneficial for all programs.
Reference counting reclaims all unreachable memory, including cyclic structures.
Closures copy the values of captured variables at creation time, so later changes are never visible.

concepts.name: JIT compilation and tiering
concepts.summary: Evaluate profile-guided JIT designs, including speculation, deoptimisation and tier trade-offs between warm-up and peak speed.

concepts.name: Optimisation correctness and undefined behaviour
concepts.summary: Assess how language semantics, undefined behaviour and memory models constrain valid transformations.

concepts.name: Interprocedural and alias analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate precision versus cost of analyses like points-to and escape analysis and their effect on optimisation.

concepts.name: Language design and implementation trade-offs
concepts.summary: Design language features such as exceptions, coroutines or pattern matching with a plan for their efficient implementation.

concepts.name: Compiler infrastructure and retargetability
concepts.summary: Design a compiler architecture with layered IRs and reusable passes that supports multiple front ends and back ends.

concepts.name: Verifying compilers and testing
concepts.summary: Evaluate approaches such as differential testing, fuzzing and formal verification for finding miscompilation.

concepts.name: Advanced parsing and incremental tooling
concepts.summary: Create parsers and front ends that support ambiguity, robust error recovery and incremental reparsing for editors.

misconceptions.text: A JIT compiler always outperforms ahead-of-time compilation because it has runtime information.
Compilers treat undefined behaviour as a platform-specific result that behaves predictably at runtime.
If a compiler passes its test suite, it is free of miscompilation bugs.
